iii-dl-01.prompt: Order the gates a new AI system passes through from first business case to shadow-mode readiness evidence.
iii-dl-01.steps[0].label: Business case & objectives
iii-dl-01.steps[0].detail: Define why AI at all: the cost-benefit case, including societal impacts, comes first. Nothing downstream can be evaluated without a stated objective to measure it against.
iii-dl-01.steps[1].label: Use case + impact assessment (leveraged from a PIA)
iii-dl-01.steps[1].detail: Scope the specific use case and run an impact assessment to anticipate and manage the harms it could cause. The best existing template to adapt is a privacy impact assessment (PIA/DPIA) — governance doesn't invent this from scratch.
iii-dl-01.steps[2].label: Design — risk-impact estimation & architecture
iii-dl-01.steps[2].detail: Design work includes estimating risk impact and choosing architecture. This is the first gate where architecture is actually decided; planning explicitly excludes it — planning sets objectives and governance approach, design picks how the system is built (; planning excludes architecture, ).
iii-dl-01.steps[3].label: Build
iii-dl-01.steps[3].detail: Construct the system against the design's risk-impact estimate and chosen architecture.
iii-dl-01.steps[4].label: Benchmark vs human experts in the same decision context
iii-dl-01.steps[4].detail: Before any pilot, measure how the system does against skilled people making the very same decisions — that comparison tells governance far more than an abstract accuracy target.
iii-dl-01.steps[5].label: Pilot — validate fairness + accuracy at controlled scale
iii-dl-01.steps[5].detail: Run a pre-deployment pilot whose primary purpose is validating fairness and accuracy on real-world data at a controlled, limited scale before full rollout.
iii-dl-01.steps[6].label: Shadow-mode run as documented readiness evidence
iii-dl-01.steps[6].detail: Run the system in parallel with the live process (shadow mode) and document the outcomes. This documented evidence — not a verbal sign-off — is what demonstrates deployment readiness (SG).

iii-dl-02.prompt: Order the risk-mitigation hierarchy from the most durable fix to the last resort.
iii-dl-02.steps[0].label: Eliminate the risk
iii-dl-02.steps[0].detail: Remove the risky feature or use case entirely — don't use AI in the high-risk context at all, the way a recruitment algorithm that keeps producing biased outcomes gets retired rather than endlessly patched. In the exam's parallel vocabulary this same top tier is called 'Avoid': stop undertaking the activity so the exposure goes to zero. Same concept, different label — defuse the vocabulary clash, don't pick a side.
iii-dl-02.steps[1].label: Substitute with a lower-risk design
iii-dl-02.steps[1].detail: If elimination isn't feasible, swap in a simpler, more interpretable model or a lower-risk dataset that achieves the same purpose — an opaque model for an interpretable one, a noisier dataset for one collected under stricter quality controls. Exam phrasing sometimes folds this into 'Mitigate' (act on likelihood or impact while the activity continues) — again, the same design move under a different word.
iii-dl-02.steps[2].label: Engineer safeguards
iii-dl-02.steps[2].detail: Build safeguards into the system itself: confidence thresholds, robustness testing, bias audits, explainability tools — and human-in-the-loop controls, which sit here as one example technique among several, not as a separate last-resort tier of their own. This is where most technical controls live, and where the exam's 'Mitigate/Reduce' bucket lands too.
iii-dl-02.steps[3].label: Warn and train users
iii-dl-02.steps[3].detail: Once the system itself is as safe as engineering can make it, the next line of defense is telling people: interpretability dashboards, plain-language warnings, and user training so people interacting with the system understand its limits. This is a distinct tier from engineering controls — it changes what the human knows, not what the system does.
iii-dl-02.steps[4].label: Accept with monitoring
iii-dl-02.steps[4].detail: Whatever risk remains after the four tiers above is knowingly accepted and watched — audit logs and post-market review, not silent tolerance. The exam's final tier, 'Accept', maps cleanly onto this one: a recorded decision, owned at the right level of authority, backed by ongoing monitoring rather than a one-time sign-off. Some frameworks insert Administrative controls as a distinct tier — the NIOSH-style hierarchy taught in Hierarchy of Controls — same idea, different slicing.

iii-dl-03.prompt: Order the steps for running a probability × severity harms matrix during design.
iii-dl-03.steps[0].label: Enumerate harms per stakeholder
iii-dl-03.steps[0].detail: List the ways the system could go wrong for each affected group — end users, downstream subjects, operators — before scoring anything. Stakeholder mapping widens the lens beyond the development team so no group's exposure is missed.
iii-dl-03.steps[1].label: Score probability × severity
iii-dl-03.steps[1].detail: Rate each enumerated harm on likelihood and impact using pre-defined scales. This scoring is applied throughout design and testing, not as a one-off exercise, so new findings can move items on the grid (SG).
iii-dl-03.steps[2].label: Prioritize — catastrophic overrides score
iii-dl-03.steps[2].detail: Rank by the plotted score, but let a catastrophic-impact item override a merely-average priority ranking: a low-likelihood, high-severity failure in an autonomous system still triggers a hard gate even if its raw score wouldn't top the list.
iii-dl-03.steps[3].label: Apply the mitigation hierarchy at the design source
iii-dl-03.steps[3].detail: Fix the highest-priority harms at the design/source level rather than bolting on disclaimers or monitoring after the fact — e.g. designing a chatbot's dialogue for crisis scenarios instead of relying on a disclaimer, or designing a model to exclude financially vulnerable customers from a harmful offer rather than flagging them after the fact.
iii-dl-03.steps[4].label: Document residual risk & owner
iii-dl-03.steps[4].detail: Record what risk remains after mitigation, at what score, and who is accountable for accepting it. An unrecorded residual risk is indistinguishable from an unmanaged one.
